title: The pain isn't touching it
objective: Recognize acute compartment syndrome from pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch and a tense compartment, then remove constricting dressings, keep the limb at heart level, support blood pressure and escalate for fasciotomy
secondaryObjectives: Compartment syndrome: early recognition and management

brief.situation: 01:00 in a trauma ICU. You are Mr. Ortiz's nurse. He is 34, admitted 10 hours ago after a motorcycle crash with a right tibial plateau fracture in a long-leg splint with a circumferential elastic wrap, awaiting surgery in the morning.
handover: He has had the ordered IV opioid three times since midnight; his pain is 10 out of 10 and 'getting worse, not better'.
His right leg is propped high on three pillows 'to help the swelling'. His MAP has drifted from 80 to 66 after the last opioid dose.

Unit policy for suspected compartment syndrome: loosen any circumferential dressing to the skin, keep the limb at heart level, support the blood pressure, and call orthopedics at once for compartment pressures and fasciotomy.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Muscle ischemia in the anterior compartment progresses. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
It slows with the wrap loosened, the leg at heart level and the pressure supported, until fasciotomy. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
More opioid lowers the pressure further and hides the pain that tracks the ischemia. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
The authored point of irreversible muscle necrosis. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Orthopedics called within 5 minutes of the passive stretch finding (unit policy).
Orthopedics measures the compartments and takes him for fasciotomy: about 30 min.

then.log: Passive stretch of his toes makes him cry out: severe pain in the front of the shin.
The anterior compartment is tense and firm, 'like wood'.
Numbness between the first and second toes; weak toe extension; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses present. Pulses do not rule it out.
Pain 6 at 20:00, now 10 despite three doses: pain out of proportion to the injury and rising.

source.note: About 30 min for orthopedics to measure and take him.

effects.log: He goes to the OR for a four-compartment fasciotomy.

why.question: Why is his pain rising, and what do you do now?

parts.label: Why
parts.criteria: Acute compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion and rising despite opioids, pain on passive stretch (most sensitive), a tense compartment and early paresthesia; pulses are a late sign and their presence does not rule it out.
parts.modelAnswer: His pain is out of proportion and climbing despite opioids, stretching his toes is agony, the front of his shin is rock hard and he's numb between his first two toes. That's compartment syndrome. His pulses being there doesn't rule it out; losing them is late.

parts.label: What now
parts.criteria: Splits circumferential dressings to the skin; brings the leg to heart level (not elevated); supports blood pressure (holds more opioid, fluid as ordered); calls orthopedics at once for pressures and fasciotomy.
parts.modelAnswer: Cut the wrap down to the skin, bring the leg down to heart level, and support his pressure: hold more opioid and run the fluid. Call orthopedics now for compartment pressures and fasciotomy.

noProgress.rationale: Suspected compartment syndrome without a surgeon an hour on is harm here.

expertPath.text: Passive toe stretch: severe pain. Anterior compartment tense.
Split the wrap to the skin; leg to heart level; hold opioid, run the fluid.
Compartment syndrome. Call orthopedics now for pressures and fasciotomy. Document.

necrosis.headline: Muscle lost
necrosis.body: Pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch and a tense compartment are compartment syndrome, pulses or not. Split dressings, keep the limb at heart level, support pressure and get the surgeon now.

decompressed.headline: Caught early
decompressed.body: You recognized it from the stretch pain and the tense compartment, split the wrap, leveled the leg, supported his pressure and called within minutes. That is the expert path.

decompressedGaps.headline: To fasciotomy, with gaps
decompressedGaps.body: Check how fast you called, whether the wrap and leg position were fixed, and whether more opioid went in.

time_up.headline: Undecompressed
time_up.body: Suspected compartment syndrome needs a surgeon within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: Rising pain out of proportion despite opioids, severe pain on passive stretch of the toes, a tense anterior compartment and early numbness in the first web space are acute compartment syndrome; present pulses do not rule it out, because loss of pulses is late. Split the circumferential wrap to the skin, bring the leg down to heart level (elevation lowers arterial inflow), and support his blood pressure by holding more opioid and giving the ordered fluid, because a low pressure narrows the gap between perfusion and compartment pressure. Call orthopedics at once for compartment pressures and fasciotomy.

signQ.ask: While you examine: which is the most sensitive early finding of compartment syndrome?

choices.label: Pain on passive stretch of the compartment's muscles

signQ.explain: Pain with passive stretch is the most sensitive exam finding; paralysis and pulselessness are late.

levelQ.ask: While he goes to the OR: why heart level and not elevated?

choices.label: Elevation lowers arterial inflow to an already squeezed compartment

levelQ.explain: Keep the limb at heart level rather than elevated, since elevation may reduce arterial perfusion.
